04-1.title: Chatbot vs agent
04-1.tldr: A chatbot maps one input to one model reply; an agent runs a loop (model → tools → results → repeat) until a stopping condition.
points: Chatbot: one model turn, no tools.
Agent: tool/reason loop with a stopping rule.
The loop and tools, not the model, define an agent.

04-2.title: Workflow vs agent
04-2.tldr: A workflow is a pre-declared graph (you author steps/edges/branches); an agent decides its next step at runtime from model output.
points: Agent: runtime branching on model output.
A workflow can embed an agent as a node.

04-3.title: Linear chain vs conditional graph
04-3.tldr: A linear chain always activates the next step; a graph adds routing (choose successors from state) and joining/barriers (when a merge node is ready).
points: Graph: conditional edges route by state.

04-4.title: ReAct pattern
04-4.tldr: ReAct alternates thought → action → observation; interleaving lets each real tool result inform the next thought, correcting drift and grounding reasoning.
points: Tool results become the next observation.
Interleaving corrects drift vs a big upfront plan.

04-5.title: Function calling under the hood
04-5.tldr: Tool schemas (name, description, JSON-Schema params) go in the request; the model returns a structured tool_calls list; the host validates args, executes, and feeds results back.
points: Send tool schemas with the request.
Host validates args, runs the tool, feeds the result back.

04-6.title: Hard iteration limit
04-6.tldr: Cap the loop with a max-iteration/round counter plus token/time budgets, enforced (not just reported), with a cap at each nesting level and configurable.
points: Cap each nested loop; make caps configurable.

04-7.title: What stops an agent
04-7.tldr: Usually the model: no tool calls means the answer is final. Around that sit hard limits — max iterations, token/time budgets, explicit stop conditions.
points: Outer loop: stop evaluators + completion promise.

04-8.title: How many retrieval hops
04-8.tldr: Use a sufficiency check to stop when evidence answers the question, and cap hops with a hard limit plus repetition and cost guards.
points: Hard hop cap as a backstop.

04-9.title: Infinite tool-calling loop
04-9.tldr: Cap iterations, detect repetition on canonicalized (tool,args), nudge or abort on no progress, and cap rounds/tokens/time.

04-10.title: Retrieve again or answer
04-10.tldr: Ask the model a sufficiency question — is the evidence enough, and if not what's the next query? Stop when sufficient or the cap is hit.
points: If not sufficient, produce the next query.
Stop on sufficient/no-next-question or the cap.

04-11.title: Registering tools
04-11.tldr: Register a tool with name, description, and parameter schema; the framework collects them into the model request in the provider's tool format; returned tool calls are dispatched.
points: Framework builds the provider tool list.
Model tool calls are parsed and dispatched.

04-12.title: Unsupported tool
04-12.tldr: Wrap an arbitrary function as a tool, define a custom tool class for special transport/auth, or connect an external tool server via a protocol like MCP.
points: Wrap any function as a tool.

04-13.title: Failed or malformed tool call
04-13.tldr: Treat failures as data: catch, classify retryable, return a structured error the model can read, and repair obvious damage (e.g., unbalanced JSON).
points: Catch and classify retryable vs not.

04-14.title: Retry without duplicate effects
04-14.tldr: Never blindly retry non-idempotent actions; mark side-effecting tools, use idempotency keys, and retry only reads or explicitly idempotent operations.

04-15.title: Custom per-tool retry policy
04-15.tldr: Retry policy should be per-tool and overridable — idempotency flag, max attempts, backoff, timeout — without silently disabling safety.

04-16.title: Concurrent tool calls
04-16.tldr: Run independent tool calls from one turn concurrently with async tasks, but bound concurrency and respect per-resource ordering.
points: Group the turn's tool calls; run them concurrently.

04-17.title: Step timeout or error
04-17.tldr: Bound each step with a timeout, classify errors, convert failures into data (an observation) so the loop can adapt, and propagate fatal errors with cleanup.
points: Convert failure into a model-readable result.

04-18.title: Task decomposition
04-18.tldr: Either ask the model to emit a plan/todo list up front, or decompose lazily and revise; store it as structured tasks that can be marked in-progress/done.
points: Store as structured tasks with status.

04-19.title: Changing the plan mid-run
04-19.tldr: Allow plan mutation during the run — add, reorder, cancel, replace tasks — and support steering with new instructions; keep the authoritative plan separate from live state.

04-20.title: Single-step vs planning agent
04-20.tldr: Two axes: single-step vs multi-step (how many model↔tool cycles) and reactive vs planning (whether an explicit plan is kept and updated).

04-21.title: Planner-executor pattern
04-21.tldr: A planner produces the steps; one or more executors carry them out, often with a supervisor re-planning — useful when planning needs a global view and execution is parallel/specialized.

04-22.title: State across steps
04-22.tldr: A state object threaded through (or held per session) that each step reads/writes; conversation history is usually separate from working state; persist via checkpoints.
points: Separate conversation history from task state.

04-23.title: Pause and resume an agent
04-23.tldr: Pause needs a durable checkpoint at a safe boundary or a first-class interrupt that unwinds the run preserving state; resume reloads the checkpoint or replays the suspended step.

04-24.title: Human-in-the-loop approval
04-24.tldr: Route sensitive steps through a permission check returning allow/ask/deny, pause on ask, surface a confirm payload, resume with the decision, and remember/persist rules; fail closed on unknown.
points: Pause on ask; resume with the decision.

04-25.title: Short vs long-term memory
04-25.tldr: Short-term is the live working context (recent turns, task state) for the next call; long-term is durable cross-session knowledge retrieved on demand.
points: Long-term is retrieved into the turn.

04-26.title: What to store vs discard
04-26.tldr: Keep durable, reused, preference-like, decision-relevant facts; discard transient chatter and stale/contradicted entries — usually extract candidates with an LLM, then dedupe/resolve.

04-27.title: Bounding memory growth
04-27.tldr: Bound on multiple axes: hard-drop/truncate oldest context, offload large blobs, compact old tool results, summarize/archive, and cap stored long-term entries.
points: Offload large blobs; compact tool results.

04-28.title: Summarizing history safely
04-28.tldr: Keep recent turns verbatim; summarize older turns into a structured note (goal, decisions, files/state, open tasks, next step) rather than free prose; re-inject durable state.

04-29.title: What a framework gives you
04-29.tldr: Raw API = request → response. A framework adds the surrounding machinery: session/state, context management, a tool registry, a control loop, streaming, tracing, and guardrails.

04-30.title: Graph vs role frameworks
04-30.tldr: Graph-based makes control flow an explicit graph of nodes/edges over shared state (deterministic, inspectable); role-based makes the unit an agent with a role that collaborates (flexible, less deterministic).
points: Role: agents with roles that collaborate.

04-31.title: Choosing a framework
04-31.tldr: Pick by control shape and state model: explicit graph/routing with durable state → LangGraph; role/team collaboration for fast multi-agent → CrewAI; a managed agent SDK for host-managed agents.
points: Managed agent SDK for hosted agents.
Match the framework to the control shape.

04-32.title: Heavier framework vs custom
04-32.tldr: Heavy frameworks give batteries (tools, memory, permissions, teams, observability) at the cost of startup time, learning curve, config surface, and churn; light custom code is transparent but you build the plumbing.
points: Choose by team size, rate of change, control needs.

04-33.title: Unnecessary abstraction
04-33.tldr: The framework adds abstraction when the app is a single model call, when its node/agent/state model forces you to reshape logic, or when the graph is actually a straight line — warning signs include fighting the framework.
points: Single model call doesn't need a framework.
Forcing business logic into nodes/agents is a smell.
A straight line disguised as a graph.

04-34.title: When abstractions don't fit
04-34.tldr: Use escape hatches: implement the base interface directly, call the primitive without the wrapper, override hooks, or replace a component; if there's no seam, that's a real limitation.
points: Call the primitive (model/tool) without the wrapper.
Override hooks or replace a component.

04-35.title: Which node runs next
04-35.tldr: A scheduler activates every node whose input channels are ready, runs them (often concurrently), routes outputs to successors, and repeats until no node is active.

04-36.title: Versioning & rolling back workflows
04-36.tldr: Treat the agent/workflow definition as a versioned artifact: immutable versions with a content hash, activate one, list history, roll back atomically — prompts are only a subset.
points: Version the whole definition, not just prompts.

04-37.title: Supervisor vs peer-to-peer
04-37.tldr: A supervisor is one controller that plans and dispatches to workers (workers-as-tools), top-down; peer-to-peer has agents share a board/bus and coordinate as equals.

04-38.title: Multi-agent communication
04-38.tldr: Either a shared blackboard (task board/state) plus a message bus, or direct messaging; messages should be persisted and ordered for auditability, with routing (direct/broadcast/mentions).

04-39.title: Agent output as another's input
04-39.tldr: Either a call returns the value (subagent/tool), a handoff transfers control and context, or a shared board/bus carries the artifact — the framework must define result and context propagation.

04-40.title: Conflicting/redundant results
04-40.tldr: Give each unit of work one owner, enforce one-active-task-per-worker, arbitrate claims atomically, reassign instead of release, dedupe dispatch, and isolate workspaces.

04-41.title: Debugging a multi-agent failure
04-41.tldr: You need per-agent attribution: a trace/span tree where every agent, model, and tool call is a span with agent identity, plus durable conversation/task history to reconstruct order.

04-42.title: When multi-agent is overkill
04-42.tldr: Multi-agent is justified when workstreams are genuinely independent, scopes differ (tools/permissions), or specialization would otherwise fight for one context; otherwise a single well-designed agent is simpler.
points: Otherwise: a single agent is simpler.

04-43.title: Agentic RAG
04-43.tldr: A fixed RAG pipeline retrieves once and feeds top-k to the generator; agentic RAG adds a decision loop — whether/when to retrieve, rewrite/decompose the query, and whether the evidence is enough.
points: Agentic: decide whether/when to retrieve again.

04-44.title: Preventing agentic RAG loops
04-44.tldr: Cap the rounds, detect repeated queries/results, require a sufficiency signal to continue, put a token/cost budget on the loop, and cache/dedupe retrieval.

04-45.title: Cost with repeated tool calls
04-45.tldr: Bound the loop (iterations/rounds/time), cap tokens, use cheaper models for cheap work, cache, and surface per-run cost; retries and huge tool outputs are hidden cost sources.
points: Cap tokens; route cheap work to small models.
Cache; watch retries and large tool outputs.
